data.name: Monstro: Battle Tactics
data.detailed_description:
On Ludus, ancient terror beasts and humans somehow coexist in perfect harmony. Yet once every few hundred years or so, a predictably unpredictable astrological phenomenon occurs wherein some angry people from the sky arrive from their dimension, "Terra". Whenever they arrive, a fleet of floating islands are brought along and make up the battlefields where the humans and the beasts battle for the amusement of the angry Skygods.

Welcome to Monstro. A fully deterministic logic game which plays like a tactical RPG but without RP, character growth or randomness. Fight the opposing army on the battlefield, which just so happens to be made up of conveniently perfect squares. Survive the onslaught and strike back to be the last one standing. Or, occasionally, do something else the evil Skygods want to be done for their own amusement.

This game takes the traditional tRPG gameplay and reconstructs it into a completely deterministic, logical experience with a twist of tactics. All of this is spiced up with ridiculous, tongue-in-cheek lore and approachable difficulty.

List of features:
- A puzzle game with completely deterministic and repeatable set of rules which still feels like playing a tRPG.
- And even though it plays like a tRPG there are no RPG elements, so it feels more like a t.
- A tongue-in-cheek plot, much better than the previous bullet point!
- No need to tediously repeat the same sequence of moves over and over if you lose, because undo is here! Undo a single move, undo all moves back to the beginning of the mission, undo if you fail the mission and even undo if you are victorious!
- Learn the rules of the enemy AI and use them for your victory. Or read them up because everything is in the in-game help!
- Real-time lighting which adds new depth to the crisp pixel art.
- Traps, pimped-up units, moving walls and breakable walls, ranged attacks and quick feedback on predicted enemy movement.
- 23 achievements including 17 which require you to complete existing levels in a more difficult way!
- 6 Trading Cards with descriptions expanding the game's weird lore.
- Skygods, hand-drawn islands, ancient terror beasts, Goos with :3 faces and the background pushed around by an artificial wind.

reviews.review:
Monstro: Battle Tactics takes the familiar appearance of a turn-based tactical RPG and transforms it into something closer to a carefully constructed logic puzzle. Developed and published by Retrocade.net, the game deliberately removes many conventions normally associated with the genre. There is no character leveling, equipment grind, random damage, or dependence on lucky outcomes. Every action follows predictable rules, placing the responsibility for victory almost entirely on the player's ability to understand the battlefield and plan several moves ahead.

The story provides an amusing excuse for these tactical encounters. Humans and ancient monsters live together on Ludus until visitors from another dimension called Terra periodically appear alongside floating islands. These islands become arenas where humans and creatures fight for the entertainment of the Skygods. The narrative never takes itself too seriously, using deliberately strange lore and playful humor to give personality to what is fundamentally a collection of tactical challenges. The unusual creatures, floating battlefields, and intentionally ridiculous concepts prevent the experience from feeling like a sterile puzzle simulator.

Combat is where the game establishes its strongest identity. Everything is deterministic, meaning identical actions under identical circumstances produce identical results. Enemy behavior can therefore be learned and anticipated rather than treated as an unpredictable obstacle. Understanding how opponents move and react becomes just as important as controlling your own units. The game even provides quick feedback concerning predicted enemy movement, allowing players to evaluate possible consequences before committing to a strategy. This creates a satisfying rhythm of observation, planning, execution, and adjustment.

Another excellent feature is the generous undo system. Tactical puzzle games can become frustrating when one small mistake forces the player to repeat several minutes of already solved actions. Here, individual moves can be reversed, while larger portions of a mission can also be rewound when necessary. Undo remains useful even after failure or victory, making experimentation considerably less punishing. Instead of treating mistakes as reasons to restart, the game encourages players to analyze why a plan failed and immediately try another solution.

Battlefields become increasingly complicated through traps, ranged attacks, enhanced units, moving walls, destructible barriers, and other environmental mechanics. These additions create situations where simply attacking the nearest opponent is rarely the smartest approach. Positioning can be used to manipulate enemy behavior, while obstacles may become either defensive tools or tactical liabilities depending on the situation. Since opponents obey understandable rules, particularly satisfying solutions often involve predicting an entire sequence of enemy actions and turning those behaviors against them.

The lack of conventional RPG progression is both an advantage and a limitation. Players cannot compensate for a difficult encounter by grinding levels or acquiring stronger equipment. Progress depends primarily on learning the mechanics and improving tactical reasoning. This makes victories feel deserved, but players who enjoy building characters, collecting loot, customizing abilities, and developing a party across a long campaign may find the experience comparatively restrictive. Monstro is ultimately more interested in testing the person playing than improving numerical statistics attached to characters.

Its pixel-art presentation complements this focused design. Crisp sprites, hand-drawn floating islands, unusual monsters, real-time lighting, and small environmental effects give the battlefields more personality than their grid-based construction might initially suggest. Visual clarity remains important because positioning is central to the gameplay. The whimsical Goos and other creatures also reinforce the game's lighthearted character. It is not visually extravagant, but the presentation serves the mechanics effectively and gives the game a recognizable identity.

There is additional replay value for completion-focused players. The game includes 23 Steam achievements, with many asking players to revisit existing missions under tougher conditions. These optional objectives can significantly change how a familiar battlefield must be approached, providing another reason to master the deterministic systems rather than simply completing every stage once. Steam Trading Cards and Steam Cloud support provide a few additional platform features.

Steam Deck compatibility is officially unverified, and the game does not carry a Steam Deck Verified or Playable rating. The available Steam version lists Windows as its supported operating system, so Deck users should treat compatibility as uncertain rather than guaranteed. Its modest hardware requirements and turn-based design may appear suitable for portable play, but those characteristics alone do not establish reliable SteamOS compatibility.

Monstro: Battle Tactics succeeds because it commits completely to its central idea. By removing randomness and traditional RPG progression, it creates tactical encounters where knowledge, prediction, and positioning determine the outcome. The extensive undo system keeps this precision from becoming excessively punishing, while the humorous setting and quirky presentation prevent the experience from becoming overly clinical. Its narrow focus will not satisfy everyone, especially players wanting deep character progression, but as a deterministic tactical puzzle game it offers a clever and unusually pure test of strategic thinking.

It is a smart, approachable, and distinctive tactical puzzler that replaces luck and grinding with predictable rules and genuine problem solving.

Rating: 7/10
